Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit 2026–27: the amounts, the 5% phase-out, the 2025 base year and the quarterly payments

A worked guide to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (formerly the GST/HST credit) for July 2026 to June 2027: the CAD 445, 234 and 234 building blocks, the 2% single supplement, the 5% reduction above CAD 46,432, why the 2025 return sets every payment, and what a reassessment or family change does. Five charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original illustration of the federal Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (CGEB, formerly the GST/HST credit) for the payment period July 2026 to June 2027, based on 2025 adjusted family net income. Parameters are derived from the CRA payments chart dated 8 June 2026 (CAD 445 adult and spouse or eligible-dependant amounts, CAD 234 per other child, single supplement up to CAD 234 phased in at 2% above CAD 11,564, all reduced by 5% above CAD 46,432) and reproduce every row of that chart. Eligibility (age 19, residence, a filed 2025 return, a registered child) is assumed. Provincial and territorial programs paid with the benefit, the separately paid Ontario trillium benefit, shared custody, mid-year changes in marital status or children, and offsets against debts are not modelled. Quarterly amounts are the annual amount divided by four; CRA rounding can differ by a cent.

The central idea

For July 2026 to June 2027 the benefit is built from CAD 445 per adult (or eligible dependant), CAD 234 per other child and a CAD 234 single supplement, then reduced by 5 cents per dollar of 2025 adjusted family net income above CAD 46,432. The 2025 return fixes the amount for the whole year; anything you change now affects the payments that start in July 2027.

01

What changed in 2026: a new name, a 25% increase and a one-time top-up

The Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (CGEB) replaced the GST/HST credit in July 2026. The CRA describes it as the same tax-free quarterly payment for people with low and modest incomes, with the same eligibility rules; the last payment under the old name was issued on 2 April 2026. The Department of Finance backgrounder of 26 January 2026 announced two changes, and the legislation was reported passed on 12 February 2026:

  • A one-time top-up equal to 50% of the annual 2025–26 GST/HST credit, issued on 5 June 2026 to people entitled to the credit in January 2026. It was based on 2024 income and the January 2026 family situation, and it did not include provincial or territorial amounts.
  • A 25% increase for five years starting with the July 2026 payments, on top of the usual inflation indexation. Finance estimated CAD 8.6 billion of extra support over 2026–27 to 2030–31.
Federal maximum annual amounts by benefit year (CRA pages reviewed 26 October 2026)

Each other child under 19CAD 184CAD 234
Single supplement (maximum)CAD 184CAD 234
Maximum · single, no childrenCAD 533CAD 679
Maximum · couple, no childrenCAD 698CAD 890

The 2025–26 column matches the CRA’s top-up page, whose maximum top-ups (CAD 267 single, CAD 349 couple, CAD 441 with one child) are half of those annual maxima, rounded. CAD 445 ÷ CAD 349 is about 1.275, consistent with 2% indexation multiplied by the 25% increase. The CRA’s summary pages state the CGEB maxima as CAD 679 single, CAD 890 couple and CAD 234 per child; the per-person blocks above are derived from its payments chart, as explained next.

02

The formula behind the CRA chart: three blocks, a 2% phase-in and a 5% reduction

The CRA publishes a payments chart for July 2026 to June 2027 rather than a formula. Every one of its 135 cells, for single and married households with zero to four or more children, is reproduced by the following parameters, which this guide derived and checked cell by cell:

CGEB parameters for July 2026–June 2027 (derived from the CRA chart dated 8 June 2026)
ParameterAmount
Adult amountCAD 445
Spouse or common-law partner amount, or for a single parent the first child (eligible-dependant amount)CAD 445
Each other eligible child under 19CAD 234
Single supplement, single person with no children2% of adjusted family net income above CAD 11,564, up to CAD 234 (reached at CAD 23,264)
Single supplement, single parentCAD 234 in full
Reduction5% of adjusted family net income above CAD 46,432

So a single person with no income gets CAD 445, which rises 2 cents per dollar from CAD 11,564 until it reaches CAD 679 at CAD 23,264. A couple with no children gets CAD 890; with one child, CAD 1,124. A single parent with one child also gets CAD 1,124 (CAD 445 + 445 + 234 supplement), which is why the chart’s one-child columns are the same for both marital statuses below the threshold.

The reduction threshold is the same for every household; children move the zero point, not the start of the phase-out. The chart labels its last column “4 children or more”, so the model stops at four children rather than assuming how larger families are shown.

Adjusted family net income (AFNI) is line 23600 for you and any spouse or common-law partner, minus Universal Child Care Benefit and RDSP income (lines 11700 and 12500), plus any of those amounts repaid (lines 21300 and 23200).

03

The 2025 return sets the whole July 2026–June 2027 year

The CRA calculates the benefit once a year from the previous year’s return. Payments from July 2026 to June 2027 use the 2025 base year; the January and April 2026 payments still used 2024 income. That has three practical consequences.

  1. The 2025 return must be filed, even with no income, and by both spouses. A late-filed earlier return can still produce a retroactive amount, now issued as a CGEB payment.
  2. Income you change today does not affect this year’s payments. An RRSP contribution made in November 2026 can only be deducted on the 2026 or a later return, so the earliest benefit it can change starts in July 2027. The parameters for that year have not been published and will be indexed again.
  3. A reassessment of 2025 that changes either spouse’s net income triggers a notice of redetermination. If the change raises income, the overpayment is recovered from future benefit payments or tax refunds; if it lowers income, the extra is paid.

Someone turning 19 during the year needs a filed 2025 return; their first payment is the quarter after the birthday. In the CRA’s example, a person turning 19 on 5 January 2027 is not eligible for the January 2027 payment but may be for April 2027.

04

Worked examples: four households under the 2026–27 amounts

Single, no children, 2025 AFNI CAD 52,000. The maximum is CAD 679. Income is CAD 5,568 above CAD 46,432, so the reduction is 5% × 5,568 = CAD 278.40 and the annual benefit is CAD 400.60, paid as four payments of CAD 100.15. If a reassessment of the 2025 return lowered AFNI by CAD 3,000 to CAD 49,000, the reduction would fall to CAD 128.40 and the benefit would rise to CAD 550.60—CAD 150.00 more, or 5 cents per dollar. These are the model’s defaults.

Single, no children, AFNI CAD 15,000. The supplement is 2% × (15,000 − 11,564) = CAD 68.72, so the benefit is CAD 513.72, or CAD 128.43 a quarter. Here extra income raises the benefit by 2 cents per dollar until CAD 23,264.

Couple with two children, AFNI CAD 40,000. Below the threshold the benefit is the full CAD 445 + 445 + 2 × 234 = CAD 1,358, or CAD 339.50 a quarter. Finance’s illustrative CAD 1,890 for this household in 2026–27 adds the June 2026 top-up (up to CAD 533 for two children) to the regular amount; budget the top-up as a one-off, not as part of the quarterly run rate.

Single, no children, AFNI CAD 57,000. The benefit is 679 − 5% × 10,568 = CAD 150.60. Because that is less than CAD 50 a quarter, the CRA pays the whole amount in July 2026, so there is nothing in October, January or April.

05

When the amount changes during the year

The annual amount is not fixed if the household changes. The CRA recalculates from the effective date when a spouse or partner relationship starts or ends, an eligible child is added or turns 19, a shared-custody arrangement starts or stops, a recipient dies, or a reassessment changes either spouse’s net income. Couples receive one payment for both, paid to whichever spouse’s return is assessed first; in shared custody each parent receives half of the child amounts.

Two cash-flow points matter more than the arithmetic. First, the benefit can be applied to amounts owed for tax, earlier benefit overpayments or other government debts, so a household with a balance owing may not receive the cash. Second, a change in marital status can move a household between the single and couple tables in either direction: a single parent with one child below the threshold receives the same CAD 1,124 as a couple with one child, but the couple’s combined income is what gets tested against CAD 46,432.

06

Budgeting with the benefit: run rate, stacking and the 5% rate

  • Use the quarterly run rate. One quarter of the annual amount arrives around the 5th of July, October, January and April. If you put it toward groceries or a utility bill, the related Canada child benefit calendar guide helps line up the two payment streams.
  • Treat the June 2026 top-up as one-off. Finance’s illustration shows 2026–27 as a peak year because of it; from 2027–28 the increase is the ongoing 25% only, and Finance describes the increase as lasting five years.
  • Count the whole stack in the phase-out. Between CAD 46,432 and the zero point, an extra dollar of 2025 income cost 5 cents of this benefit on top of income tax, payroll contributions and other income-tested benefits such as the Canada child benefit, the Canada workers benefit and provincial credits. The model shows only this benefit’s share.
  • Add provincial amounts separately. Several provincial and territorial credits are paid with the federal benefit (for example New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan programs); the Ontario sales tax credit is paid separately as part of the Ontario trillium benefit. None of them is included here.

07

What the official 2025–26 payment statistics show

The CRA’s statistics for July 2025 to June 2026, the last year under the GST/HST credit name, report 54,827,530 payments totalling CAD 9,846,224,000, including related provincial and territorial program payments (page dated 19 October 2026, counts rounded to the nearest ten and amounts to the nearest thousand dollars). The first three quarters each paid about CAD 1.7 billion in roughly 10.7 to 10.9 million payments. The April–June 2026 quarter paid CAD 4,698,827,000 in 22,270,170 payments.

The CRA table does not split out the one-time top-up, so this guide does not attribute an exact amount to it. The jump is consistent with the top-up’s 5 June 2026 issue date falling in that quarter. The figures are observations of payments made, not of entitlement, and the CRA notes that they are subject to change as returns are processed.

08

Limits of the model

The model applies one set of federal parameters to one household for the whole payment period. It assumes the eligibility conditions are met and leaves out provincial and territorial programs, shared custody, mid-year changes, debts offset against payments, and households with more than four children. Parameters are derived from the CRA chart rather than quoted from a CRA formula, and quarterly amounts are the annual amount divided by four, so a cent of rounding can differ. Check your CRA account or the CRA child and family benefits calculator for your actual entitlement.
